4x payment
success.

A $750M-a-year payment service converting only 9%, running on a backend that couldn’t be touched. The checkout redesign took the success rate from 11% to 43% in key markets, and tripled it overall, to 27%.

RolePrincipal Product Designer, first and only, reporting to the CPO

Shipped

The flagship, much improved.

Confirmo had never had a designer, and it showed. Built to an engineering spec and named after the technical outcome, Invoices converted only 9%.

The real problem was underneath: the flow was running backwards, and the backend was off limits due to crippling legacy code.

Before: 9% completed payments.
After: 27% globally, 43% in key markets.

I couldn’t change anything, so I had to optimize everything.

Unable to change the foundations, I had to create on the surface. Dozens of small improvements added up, improving the flow as a whole. It was the same, but better, and the results proved it: 43% in key markets, 27% globally, adding $135M on the same $750M volume as before.

v0.0

Initial audit and workshops.

The live product when I arrived lost 9 of every 10 payments. First, I mapped exactly what worked and what leaked.

  • Week 1: audited full product flows (20+ screens), and analytics.
  • Week 2: workshops with Sales, Engineering, Product and Support, going over tickets and real user feedback.
  • Found: almost 80 individual problems with current flow.
  • Most requested: The Payments Back Button.
Easy fix?Users are able to go back to first screen, but not back to second.

v1.0

The yellow wireframe.

Let’s start with the yellow elephant: this is a painted wireframe, never meant to ship. I used it to pitch 59 changes to the Product team, each tied to an issue from the audit, with metrics and support tickets where I had them.

Most were approved. The ones that touched the backend were not.

RejectedI proposed handling this case in the flow. Users closing the window in frustration was very common.

End states. Partially approved

  • Processing: the screen gave no useful info and could idle without failing, leaving users stuck. I proposed a Cancel. It could not be built.
  • Try again: an expired payment had no way to retry, so I designed one. It was rejected. Like most edge cases, it hit a backend limit that was not up for negotiation.
  • Payment success: what little success the flow had, it didn’t show it, leaving users frustrated even when everything worked. The backend allowed it, so I added a Success state at the end.
Payment detailsSeeing this prevented users from changing selection. Which in turn made Back impossible.

The Back Button. Rejected

The most requested fix was a back button on the payment screen. It could not be built.

Three quarters of a billion dollars a year reached the checkout. Rebuilding its backend mid-flight was a risk nobody would take, so it stayed off-limits.

One tap on a token and network locked the exchange rate, created the Invoice, linked an address to it and pushed the user onto the payment screen.

Once the payment details were on screen, an Invoice had to exist to match them. Changing the selection after that could break the payment. I needed another way.

v2.0

The breadcrumbs.

At 9%, the goal was speed: moving the needle mattered more than knowing what moved it. So I loaded this version with as many changes as it could carry and shipped them together, as a live test in our 2 key markets. Every release went there first, where we performed best: a dip could be rolled back fast, and a gain made the case for everywhere else. It moved: the success rate there rose from 11% to 16%.

Crumbled signal.

I tried breadcrumbs in place of a warning label. A label telling users they could not go back would shout at everyone, including those who never needed to.

The breadcrumbs showed progress and the steps to go. They failed: users got a new target to rage click, and crumb 2 was the favourite. My mistake, and the clue: going back wasn’t the problem, being pushed onto the payment screen was.

v3.0

Full rollout.

The test results were good, but our CEO wanted more of the brand in it. I disagreed, and compromised: the brand came back, the new mechanics stayed. It turned out well, because it separated the mechanics from the look.

Stop pushing.

I couldn’t give users a back button, so I gave them a forward button. The old flow moved on the moment a network was tapped, and trapped people there. Now the user decides when to move. It costs one more tap, and traps fewer.

v4.0

Craft, matured.

This iteration refined the last one: the same flow, with polish and craft. It also let me mature the design system, the first Confirmo ever had. It covers the full checkout, 20+ screens, and stayed small by reusing first and creating new only when needed.

AsleepAdds guidance.
WakingPreviews converted price.
LiveFull summary.
Drawer controlShow/hide full breakdown.

Matured.

One button now did three jobs. It guided the first steps. It absorbed the navigation push. And it kept the price in sight through the whole flow, with more detail as it became available, because users had been sending wrong amounts and wrong tokens.

The back button turned out to be impossible. But I still tried to fix it.Users still got stuck once they moved forward. But choosing when to move took away the helplessness and, more importantly, the fear of engaging with the product. That step stayed our biggest drop-off in the data. Support tickets about it fell sharply.

Branded.

I made branding self-serve: a client gives one primary colour and an optional accent, and colour maths derives the rest. It was the last thing I built before Confirmo went all in on AI, which would have made it much easier.

1-2 punchBottom timer starts muted grey, turning red at 2:59. The top warning is pushed at 1:29.
The yellow pillA relaxed cadence, calmly indicating the user’s progress.
Desktop affordanceThe background compensates for a larger distance to the user’s sight, making it easier to track when copying details to a phone.
Permanent, toned.Another warning vying for attention. A permanent warning should be seen, without shouting. Otherwise it’ll train the user to ignore it.

Paying attention.

I held colour back, because colour is what guides the eye.

The exception is the timers. Two of them, shouting from both ends of the screen, still feels like overkill. But in crypto a lost payment costs adoption, and nothing else stopped a user from paying an expired Invoice. I traded restraint for assurance.

v5.0

Common ground.

I had worked out a one-click payment version of Checkout, for when the backend resources were made available. The trick that makes it possible was to start with the wallet, rather than leaving it to the end. An insight that gave the Subscriptions work a great head start.

Connect and tap pay. That’s all.

Connect the wallet first, and the checkout offers only the tokens it holds, on the right network. In the checkout it stayed my concept.

  1. 01Pick token.
  2. 02Pick network.
  3. 03Connect wallet, or paste.
  4. 04Tap pay.

Shipped · 4 user steps

  1. 01Connect wallet.
  2. Reads balances.
  3. Preselects most used pair.
  4. Creates Invoice on confirm.
  5. Matches the payment.
  6. 02Tap pay.

Wallet first · 2 user steps

Wallet-first wouldn’t have needed a back button.

Built with AI

A brand new product.

Subscriptions launched as Confirmo’s first new product in almost a decade, in partnership with Circle and Solana. Designed in under a month, it was built on a foundation of insights that made its flagship successful, and was a testing ground for new AI processes.

Prompted: from wireframe to high fidelity in days.

I used Claude Code to speed up the output, from the PRD to the first wireframes. The time it saved went into the prototype.

not to fix it.
